intro: Blocks on the rug. A coat on the floor. A plant with droopy leaves. A dog bowl that is empty. These are all jobs that someone started and did not finish. Every home and every classroom has them.

In this unit you learn that a job has three parts. Get it out. Do it. Put it back. The third part is the one people forget. You also learn how to take care of clothes, pets, plants, books and borrowed things.
By the end, you will know how to finish a job all the way. You will know what needs care every day. And you will know what it means to be someone people can count on.
bigQuestion: What does it take to finish a job and take care of what we have?

timeline.t: You get out the blocks. You build a tower. You put every block back in the bin.
You take off your coat and hang it on its hook. It is there when you need it.
Your shirt comes off. It goes in the laundry basket, not under the bed.
You touch the plant's soil. It is dry. You pour a half cup of water on the soil.
The dog bowl is empty. One scoop of food. Fresh water. Same time as yesterday.
Milk spills on the table. You wipe it right away and rinse the cloth.
You fold your clean clothes. Flat, side, side, bottom. Into the drawer.
The library book goes back on time, with a bookmark and no juice rings.
You ask, How can I help? Your name goes on the helper chart.
You do what you said. People know they can count on you.

words.d: one piece of a bigger job; every job has three
finished all the way, with everything put back
a box or tub that is the home for one kind of thing
putting things in groups by kind
a list on the wall that shows who does what
clothes that need washing
liquid or food that lands where it should not be
to trust that someone will do what they said

test.q: What are the three parts of a job?
choices: Get it out, do it, put it back
test.why: Every job has three parts, and the last one is putting things back.

test.q: Which part of a job do people forget most?
test.why: Put it back is the part people skip, and it matters most.

test.q: You need four crayons. What do you get out?
test.why: Get out only what you need. Less out means less to put back.

test.q: Cars and blocks are mixed in one pile. What is the fast way to clean up?
choices: Sort one kind at a time
Pick up one thing at a time in any order
Push the pile into a corner
test.why: Sorting by kind is faster and helps you find things later.
A hook keeps a coat clean and easy to find.

test.q: What does a helper chart do?
choices: Tells you what is for lunch
test.why: A chart lists a name next to each job so nothing is forgotten.

test.q: How do you know a plant needs water?
choices: The soil is dry when you touch it
test.why: Dry soil means water. Wet soil means wait.

test.q: What do you do with a pet's water bowl every day?
choices: Empty it, rinse it, fill it fresh
test.why: Fresh, clean water every day keeps a pet healthy.

test.q: A glass breaks on the floor. What do you do?
choices: Step back and tell a grown-up
test.why: Broken glass is a grown-up job because it can cut you.

test.q: What makes someone a person you can count on?
test.why: Trust grows when a person does what they said, every time.

write.prompt: Pick one job at home, like feeding a pet, making your bed or cleaning up toys. Draw or write the three parts of the job. For each part, say what you do and why it matters.
tips: Put the three parts in order: get it out, do it, put it back.
Name the tool or the home for each part: the scoop, the bin, the hook.
Say the safety rule if there is one, like a grown-up cleans up glass.
Say what would go wrong if you skipped the last part.

title: A Job Done to the End

chapters.title: Get It Out, Do It, Put It Back
chapters.bigQuestion: When is a job really done?

story.title: The Block Corner Nobody Wanted
story.kicker: The tower was fun to build. The blocks on the floor were not fun at all.
paragraphs: Free time was over. Ms. Ruiz rang the bell. Sam and Ava had built a tall tower in the block corner. Now the blocks were all over the rug. Long ones. Short ones. Round ones.
Sam walked to the reading rug. Ava went to get a drink. Nobody looked at the blocks. Nobody wanted that job. The blocks just sat there.
Ms. Ruiz stood by the block bin. "You got the blocks out," she said. "You built with them. That is two parts. A job has three parts. What is the third?"
Sam looked at the empty bin. "Put them back," he said. Ava came over. They sorted the blocks by shape. Long ones in the front. Round ones in the back. The bin was full. Now the job was done.
story.think: Why did nobody want to put the blocks back? What made the job done?

lessons.title: Get It Out
lessons.mainIdea: Every job starts by getting out only what you need.
reading: Picture a box of crayons on a shelf. You want to color. You get the box. You get one sheet of paper. That is the first *part* of the job.
Get out only what you need. Do not dump the whole bin. If you need six blocks, take six. A big pile is hard to put back.
Look before you start. Is there room? Is the table clear? Now you are ready for part two.

words.d: one piece of a bigger job

look.title: The Crayon Box
look.text: Look at Leo. He wants to color one picture. He tips the whole crayon tub onto the table. Crayons roll off the edge. Two fall on the floor. He picks up a red one and starts to color.
look.prompt: What should Leo have done instead? What will be hard for him later?

check.q: What is the first part of every job?
check.why: A job starts by getting out what you need, and only that.

check.q: You need six blocks. What do you take?
check.why: Take only what you need. A big pile is hard to put back.

check.q: Why not dump the whole tub?
choices: A big pile is hard to put back
check.why: What comes out must go back. Less out means less to put away.

lessons.title: Do It
lessons.mainIdea: The middle part of a job is the work, and you finish the work before you stop.
reading: Now you color. Or build. Or set the table. This is part two. This is the *work*. It is the part people like best.
Do the work all the way. If you set the table, set every place. Do not stop at three plates when four people eat.
If you get stuck, ask. Say, "I need help with this part." Then keep going until the work is done.

words.d: the doing part of a job

look.title: Four Plates, Three Set
look.text: Look at the table. Four people will eat dinner. Nia set three plates, three forks and three cups. Then she saw her brother playing and went to join him. One chair has nothing in front of it.
look.prompt: Is the work done? What should Nia do before she plays?

check.q: Four people will eat. How many plates do you set?
choices: As many as you feel like
check.why: Do the work all the way. Every person gets a place.

check.q: You get stuck in the middle of a job. What do you do?
choices: Ask for help and keep going
check.why: Asking for help lets you finish the work.

check.q: Which part of a job is the work?
check.why: Get it out, do it, put it back. The work is the middle part.

lessons.title: Put It Back
lessons.mainIdea: A job is not done until everything is back where it belongs.
reading: You are done coloring. The picture is finished. But the crayons are on the table. Is the job *done*? Not yet.
Put the crayons in the box. Close the lid. Put the box on the shelf. Now the job is done. Now the table is ready for the next person.
This is the part people forget. It is the part that matters most. A job with no part three leaves a mess for someone else.

words.d: finished all the way, with everything put back

look.title: Is It Done?
look.text: Look at the art table. The painting is dry and pinned on the wall. The paint cups are still open. Two brushes sit in dirty water. The smock hangs off the back of a chair. The painter has gone outside to play.
look.prompt: Which part of this job is missing? Name three things that still need to happen.

check.q: Your picture is finished. Crayons are on the table. Is the job done?
choices: No, the crayons are not put back
Yes, someone else will clean up
check.why: A job is done when everything is back where it belongs.

check.q: Which part of a job do people forget most?
check.why: Put it back is the part people skip. It is the part that matters most.

check.q: What happens if you skip part three?
check.why: A mess left behind is a problem for the next person.

lessons.title: Bins, Hooks and Shelves
lessons.mainIdea: Everything has a home, and a home makes putting back easy.
reading: Look at a coat hook by the door. Look at a *bin* with a picture of blocks on it. Look at a shelf for books. Each one is a home for something.
When a thing has a home, putting it back is easy. You do not have to think. The coat goes on the hook. The blocks go in the bin.
When a thing has no home, it ends up on the floor. Then it gets lost or stepped on. A home keeps things safe.

words.d: a box or tub that holds one kind of thing
a curved holder on a wall for hanging things

look.title: Things With a Home
look.cite: example counts from one classroom corner
look.prompt: Which home holds the most things? Why is a bin better than the floor for forty blocks?

check.q: Where does a coat go when you come inside?
check.why: A hook is the coat's home. It stays clean and easy to find.

check.q: Why does a bin have a picture on it?
check.why: The picture tells you the bin's job, even if you cannot read yet.

check.q: What happens to a thing with no home?
choices: It ends up on the floor
check.why: Things with no home get dropped, lost or stepped on.

lessons.title: Sorting as You Go
lessons.mainIdea: Sorting things by kind makes putting away faster and finding them later easier.
reading: Picture a pile of toys. Cars, blocks and puzzle pieces all mixed up. Putting them away one by one is slow.
Try this. Pick one kind first. All the cars go in the car bin. Then all the blocks. Then the puzzle pieces. This is called *sorting*.
Sorting is faster. It also helps later. Next time you want a car, you know just where to look.

words.d: putting things in groups by kind

look.title: The Mixed-Up Pile
look.text: Look at the rug. There are five toy cars, ten blocks and twelve puzzle pieces in one big pile. Three bins sit nearby. One has a car picture. One has a block picture. One has a puzzle picture.
look.prompt: Which kind would you pick up first? How would you know when the whole pile is sorted?

check.q: Cars, blocks and puzzle pieces are in one pile. What is the fast way to put them away?
choices: One toy at a time, any order
Pick one kind at a time
Push the pile under the couch
check.why: Sorting by kind is faster than picking up one mixed thing at a time.

check.q: Why does sorting help later?
check.why: When each kind has its own bin, finding a toy is quick.

check.q: What does sorting mean?
choices: Putting things in groups by kind
check.why: Sorting is putting like things with like things.

sections.title: Jobs at Home and at School

lessons.title: Dishes, Clothes and a Bed
lessons.mainIdea: Home jobs like dishes, clothes and a bed follow the same three parts.
reading: After you eat, your *dish* is still on the table. Carry it to the sink with two hands. Scrape it if a grown-up shows you how. Now the table is clear.
Clean clothes go in the drawer. Dirty clothes go in the basket. Not on the floor. Not under the bed.
A bed is a job too. Pull the sheet up flat. Pull the blanket up. Put the pillow at the top. Three steps and it is done.

words.d: a plate, bowl or cup you eat or drink from

look.title: Making a Bed
look.text: Here are the steps for a bed, but they are mixed up. Put the pillow at the top. Pull the blanket up. Pull the sheet up flat.
look.prompt: Put the three steps in the right order. What would go wrong if you put the pillow on first?

check.q: Where do dirty clothes go?
check.why: The basket is the home for dirty clothes until wash day.

check.q: What is the first step in making a bed?
check.why: The sheet goes first, then the blanket, then the pillow.

check.q: How do you carry your dish to the sink?
choices: By sliding it across the floor
check.why: Two hands keep a dish from dropping and breaking.

lessons.title: The Helper Chart
lessons.mainIdea: A helper chart shows who does which job so nothing gets forgotten.
reading: Look at the wall by the classroom door. There is a *chart*. It has names and jobs. Line leader. Plant waterer. Table wiper.
A chart makes jobs fair. Everyone gets a turn. No one has to guess. You look, find your name, and do your job.
You can make one at home too. Feed the cat. Set the table. Put shoes by the door. Ask, "How can I help?" Then add it to the chart.

words.d: a list on the wall that shows who does what

look.title: Our Class Helper Chart
look.cite: example helper chart for one week
look.prompt: Which job needs the most helpers? Why might wiping tables need two people?

check.q: What does a helper chart show?
check.why: A chart lists names next to jobs so nothing is forgotten.

check.q: Why is a chart fair?
choices: Only the fastest kid gets a job
check.why: A chart gives each person a job and switches turns.

check.q: What can you say at home to find a job?
check.why: Asking how you can help is how you find a job and become a helper.

review.q: What are the three parts of every job?
choices: Get it out, do it, put it back
review.why: Every job has three parts. The last one is putting things back.

review.q: You built a tower. The blocks are on the rug. What is left?
choices: Put the blocks back in the bin
review.why: The job is not done until the blocks are back in their home.

review.q: You want one sheet of paper. What do you get out?
review.why: Get out only what you need. Less out means less to put back.
A hook is the coat's home. It keeps it clean and easy to find.

review.q: A pile has cars and blocks mixed up. What is the fast way to clean it?
choices: Pick up one toy at a time, any order
Sort by kind, one kind at a time
review.why: Sorting by kind is faster and helps you find toys later.

review.q: Which step comes last when making a bed?
review.why: Sheet, blanket, pillow. The pillow goes on last.

chapters.title: Taking Care of Things
chapters.bigQuestion: What does it mean to be someone people can count on?

story.title: The Plant Everyone Forgot
story.kicker: A little green plant sat by the window. It needed just one thing.
paragraphs: Room 4 had a plant. It sat on the windowsill in a red pot. Its leaves were shiny and green. Everyone liked it. Everyone said they would water it.
Monday came. Nobody watered it. Tuesday. Wednesday. Each kid thought someone else would do it. On Thursday the leaves were droopy. On Friday they were curling at the edges.
Jaden saw the plant and stopped. "It is thirsty," he said. He got the small cup and filled it halfway. He poured the water slowly on the soil, not the leaves. Then he put the cup back.

Ms. Ruiz wrote Jaden's name on the helper chart next to a picture of a plant. "Now it is one person's job," she said. "When it is everyone's job, it is no one's job." By Monday, the leaves stood up again.
story.think: Why did the plant go five days with no water when everyone said they would water it?

lessons.title: Hang It or Fold It
lessons.mainIdea: Clothes last longer when you hang them or fold them instead of dropping them.
reading: You take off your jacket. Where does it go? Not on the floor. Picture the hook by the door. Hang the jacket by its loop or its collar.
A shirt can be folded. Lay it flat. *Fold* one side in. Fold the other side in. Fold the bottom up. Now it is a small square. It fits in the drawer.
Clothes on the floor get stepped on. They get wrinkled and dirty. Hung and folded clothes stay clean and ready.

words.d: to bend cloth over on itself so it is flat and small

look.title: Folding a Shirt
look.text: Here are the steps to fold a shirt, but they are mixed up. Fold the bottom up. Lay the shirt flat. Fold the other side in. Fold one side in.
look.prompt: Put the four steps in order. Which step must always come first?

check.q: What is the first step in folding a shirt?
check.why: You lay the shirt flat first. Then you fold the sides and the bottom.

check.q: Where does a jacket go when you take it off?
check.why: A hook keeps the jacket clean and off the floor.

check.q: What happens to clothes left on the floor?
choices: They get stepped on and dirty
check.why: Floor clothes get wrinkled, dirty and stepped on.

lessons.title: The Laundry Basket
lessons.mainIdea: Dirty clothes go in the basket so wash day is easy.
reading: Look at the *laundry* basket in the corner. It has one job. It holds dirty clothes until wash day.
Socks go in the basket. Shirts go in the basket. Not under the bed. Not in the toy box. If it is dirty, it goes in.
On wash day, a grown-up carries the basket to the washer. If clothes are all over the room, some get missed. Then you have no clean socks.

words.d: clothes that need washing, or the job of washing them

look.title: Where Are the Socks?
look.text: Look at Rosa's room on wash day. Two socks are under the bed. One shirt is in the toy box. A sweater is on the chair. The laundry basket has only one sock in it. Dad picks up the basket and walks to the washer.
look.prompt: What will Rosa find on Monday morning? What should she have done all week?

check.q: Where do dirty socks go?
check.why: The basket holds dirty clothes so none get missed on wash day.

check.q: Why do clothes on the floor cause a problem on wash day?
choices: They get missed and stay dirty
check.why: A grown-up washes what is in the basket. Missed clothes stay dirty.

check.q: What is the laundry basket's one job?
check.why: The basket is the home for dirty clothes until wash day.

lessons.title: Food and Water for a Pet
lessons.mainIdea: A pet cannot feed itself, so its food and water are a job you do every day.
reading: Picture a dog bowl on the floor. It is empty. The dog looks at you. The dog cannot open the food bag. That is your job.
Ask a grown-up how much food. Use the scoop. Fill the bowl that much, not more. Then check the water bowl. Empty it, rinse it and fill it with fresh water.
A *pet* needs this every day. Not just when you remember. Pick a time, like after breakfast. Do it at the same time each day.

words.d: an animal that lives with a family and depends on it
a cup used to measure out the same amount each time

look.title: One Day of Pet Care
look.cite: example care plan for one family's pets
look.prompt: Which jobs happen twice a day? Why might water need to be checked more often on a hot day?

check.q: How much food do you put in the bowl?
choices: As much as the dog wants
The amount a grown-up shows you
check.why: Too much food can make a pet sick. Use the scoop and the right amount.

check.q: What do you do with the water bowl?
choices: Empty it, rinse it, fill it fresh
Leave it until it is empty
check.why: Fresh, clean water every day keeps a pet healthy.

check.q: When should you feed a pet?
choices: At the same time every day
check.why: A pet counts on you every day. A set time helps you remember.

lessons.title: Watering a Plant
lessons.mainIdea: A plant needs the right amount of water on its soil, on a regular day.
reading: Look at the plant by the window. Touch the *soil* with one finger. Is it dry? Then it needs water. Is it wet? Then wait.
Fill a small cup halfway. Pour slowly on the soil, not on the leaves. Stop when you see water come out the bottom of the pot. Too much water can hurt a plant just like too little.
Pick a day. Check it every Monday and Thursday. Write it on the chart. Then the plant never has a droopy week.

words.d: the dirt in a pot that holds a plant's roots

look.title: Two Plants, Two Problems
look.text: Look at two plants. The first has dry, crumbly soil and droopy leaves. The second sits in a saucer full of water. Its soil is soggy and its bottom leaves are yellow.
look.prompt: What does each plant need? Why is more water not always the answer?

check.q: How do you know if a plant needs water?
choices: Touch the soil to see if it is dry
Look at the color of the pot
check.why: Dry soil means water. Wet soil means wait.

check.q: Where do you pour the water?
check.why: Roots in the soil drink the water. Leaves do not.

check.q: Can too much water hurt a plant?
check.why: Too much water leaves soil soggy and can turn leaves yellow.

lessons.title: Wipe It Now
lessons.mainIdea: A spill wiped right away is a small job; a spill left alone becomes a big one.
reading: You pour milk. Some spills on the table. Do not walk away. Get a cloth or a paper towel. Wipe it now. Rinse the cloth.
A spill on the floor is slippery. Someone can fall. Tell a grown-up if it is big or if there is broken glass. Broken glass is a grown-up job.
A *spill* left alone gets sticky. It draws ants. It dries hard. Then it takes ten wipes instead of one.

words.d: liquid or food that lands where it should not be

look.title: Juice on the Floor
look.text: Look at the kitchen. A cup of juice tipped over. Juice runs across the counter and drips onto the floor. Kai looks at it and heads for the couch. His little sister is walking toward the kitchen in socks.
look.prompt: What could happen next? What should Kai do first, and what should he say?

check.q: Milk spills on the table. What do you do?
choices: Wipe it now with a cloth
check.why: A fresh spill takes one wipe. A dry spill takes many.

check.q: Why is a spill on the floor a safety problem?
check.why: Wet floors are slippery. Wipe it before someone walks there.

check.q: A glass breaks on the floor. Whose job is it?
check.why: Broken glass can cut you. Step back and tell a grown-up.

lessons.title: Books and Borrowed Things
lessons.mainIdea: Take care of borrowed things and return them on time and in good shape.
reading: You *borrow* a library book. It is not yours. It is everyone's. Turn pages by the corner. Use a bookmark, not a fold. Keep it away from juice.
A borrowed toy or game goes back to its owner. Give it back on time. Give it back the way you got it. Say, "Thank you for letting me use it."
If something breaks, tell the truth. Say, "I am sorry, it broke." People forgive a mistake. They do not forget a hidden one.

words.d: to use something that belongs to someone else and give it back
a strip of paper that holds your place in a book

look.title: The Library Book
look.text: Look at the library book on the kitchen table. It is due tomorrow. One page corner is folded down to save the place. A ring of juice sits on the cover. The book is under a plate of toast.
look.prompt: Name three things that should be different. What does the book need before it goes back?

check.q: How do you hold your place in a library book?
check.why: A bookmark saves the page without bending or hurting the book.

check.q: You borrowed a toy and it broke. What do you do?
choices: Tell the truth and say sorry
check.why: Telling the truth is how people learn they can trust you.

check.q: What do you say when you return a borrowed thing?
choices: Thank you for letting me use it
check.why: Thank you shows you know it was a gift to use it.

lessons.title: Counting on You
lessons.mainIdea: When you do what you said you would do, people can count on you.
reading: Jaden said he would water the plant. He did. Every Monday and Thursday. Nobody had to remind him. That makes Jaden someone you can *count on*.
Counting on someone means you can trust them. You say you will feed the cat. You feed the cat. You say you will put the blocks back. You do it.
It is not about being big or fast. It is about doing what you said. Small jobs, done every time. That is how trust grows.

words.d: to trust that someone will do what they said

look.title: Who Would You Pick?
look.text: Two kids want the job of feeding the class fish. Mia fed it last week but forgot two days. Theo has been the door holder all month and never missed a day. The fish needs food every single day.
look.prompt: Who would you pick and why? What could Mia do to become someone people count on?

check.q: What does it mean to count on someone?
choices: You can trust them to do what they said
check.why: Counting on someone means trusting them to follow through.

check.q: How does trust grow?
choices: By doing small jobs every time
check.why: Trust comes from doing what you said, again and again.

check.q: You said you would feed the cat. What makes you someone people count on?
choices: Asking someone else to do it
check.why: Doing what you said is what makes people trust you.

review.q: Why did the class plant go a whole week without water?
choices: Everyone thought someone else would do it
review.why: When a job is everyone's, it is no one's. One name on the chart fixes that.

review.q: Where do you pour water for a plant?
review.why: The roots in the soil drink the water.

review.q: How much food goes in the pet bowl?
choices: As much as it will eat
review.why: Use the scoop and the right amount. Too much can make a pet sick.

review.q: Juice spills on the floor. What do you do first?
review.why: A fresh spill wipes up fast, and a wet floor can make someone fall.

review.q: You broke a borrowed toy. What do you do?
choices: Tell the truth and say sorry
Give it back and say nothing
review.why: Telling the truth is how people learn to trust you.

review.q: What is the first step in folding a shirt?
review.why: Lay it flat first. Then fold the sides and the bottom.
